dataset.what_one_row_represents: One animal-stay: an intake event paired with its eventual outcome at Long Beach Animal Care Services.
dataset.geographic_scope: City of Long Beach, CA plus contracted neighbours (Cerritos, Signal Hill, Los Alamitos, Seal Beach)

ana_01.label: Annual intake — pandemic V-curve
ana_01.content: Annual shelter intakes cratered during the pandemic. Long Beach took in 4,826 animals in 2017 and 4,429 in 2018. Intakes then drifted down through 2019 (4,176) before collapsing to 2,421 in 2020 and a record-low 1,842 in 2021 — only 38% of the 2017 baseline. Intakes then climbed back: 3,673 in 2022, 4,009 in 2023, and 4,411 in 2024, essentially restoring the pre-pandemic level. The two-year intake trough (2020-2021) is consistent with the national pattern documented by Shelter Animals Count, which attributes the drop primarily to fewer strays being found during stay-at-home orders rather than to fewer animals in distress.

data_table.description: Animals taken into LBACS by intake year, 2017-2024

ana_02.label: Adoptions tripled from 2018 to 2024
ana_02.content: Adoptions by outcome year went from 448 in 2017 and 464 in 2018 — the pre-Compassion-Saves baseline — up to 657 in 2019 (the year the model was adopted), then dipped to 506 in 2020 and a low of 365 in 2021 (when there were simply fewer animals in the building to adopt out), before exploding to 1,155 in 2022, 1,232 in 2023, and 1,463 in 2024. That is a 3.15x increase over the 2018 baseline and the highest yearly total in the dataset, matching the City's own announcement that 2024 was its highest adoption year ever.

data_table.description: Adoptions by outcome year (outcome_type='adoption'), 2017-2024

ana_03.label: Cat+dog live-release rate by year
ana_03.content: Restricting to cats and dogs (the population the 90% no-kill benchmark is defined for), the live-release rate at LBACS rose from 81.3% in 2017 and 78.3% in 2018 — both below the 90% benchmark — to 86.9% in 2019 (the Compassion Saves year) and a peak of 92.2% in 2020, the only year in the dataset that crosses the no-kill threshold. The rate then settled at 84.7% (2021), 83.5% (2022), 82.8% (2023), and 84.6% (2024). Even with record adoptions in 2024, the live-release rate has not returned to its 2020 pandemic-quiet peak; the absolute number of saves grew while the percentage moved sideways, because intake volume also grew.

data_table.description: Cat+dog live-release rate by outcome year vs the 90% no-kill benchmark

ana_04.label: Outcome composition shift — euthanasia almost halved
ana_04.content: Annual outcome buckets show how the mix moved. Euthanasia for all species fell from 1,001 in 2017 and 1,055 in 2018 to 581 in 2019, then 343 in 2020, 355 in 2021, 690 in 2022, 702 in 2023, and 724 in 2024 — roughly a 30% drop versus the 2017-2018 baseline despite intake recovering. Adoptions tripled (see ana_02). 'Rescue/transfer' (animal moved to a partner rescue or jurisdiction) is the largest single bucket and stayed roughly flat at 1,300-2,300 per year. Return-to-owner ranges 237-567 per year and tracks intake volume.

data_table.description: Annual outcome composition (counts) by bucket, 2017-2024

ana_05.label: Kitten season — May/June peak
ana_05.content: Animal intake at LBACS shows a strong seasonal peak in late spring. Total monthly intakes peak at 3,297 in June and 3,235 in May, with a December low of 1,633. The seasonality is almost entirely driven by 'kitten season': underage cats (intake_condition='under age/weight', animal_type='cat') jump from 40 in January to 901 in May — a 22.5x swing — and exceed 500/month from April through October. June alone brings in 666 underage kittens, more than the entire November-February stretch combined. Kitten season is the operational reason shelters lean so heavily on foster networks and bottle-feeding programs from April to October.

ana_06.label: Species mix — cats are nearly half the shelter
ana_06.content: The shelter is dominated by cats and dogs but is far from cat-and-dog-only. Cats account for 14,145 records (47.5%), dogs 9,768 (32.8%), birds 2,075 (7.0%), 'wild' animals (raccoons, opossums, hawks, etc.) 1,412 (4.7%), 'other' (mostly small mammals and exotic pets) 1,332 (4.5%), rabbits 526 (1.8%), reptiles 344 (1.2%), guinea pigs 172 (0.6%), with a tail of 10 livestock and 3 amphibians. The non-cat-non-dog species together — 5,864 records, 19.7% of the shelter — illustrate that an open-admission municipal shelter is also a regional wildlife triage center and exotic-pet rescue clearinghouse.

data_table.description: Animal type composition, all years

ana_08.label: Outcome destinies are species-specific
ana_08.content: Where you go after the shelter depends heavily on what species you are. Dogs predominantly go home: 29.7% return to owner, 26.6% are adopted, 19.5% transfer to a partner organisation, only 6.7% are euthanised. Cats, in contrast, rarely go back to an owner (2.2%): 27.7% are pulled by rescues, 24.4% adopted, 18.8% euthanised, 11.9% transferred, with 9.2% leaving via TNR ('shelter, neuter, return' + 'community cat' + 'trap, neuter, release'). Birds are most often transferred to a partner (34.7%) or rescue (25.2%), with euthanasia at 24.8% reflecting non-survivable injuries. 'Wild' animals are euthanised 62.2% of the time — the closest thing the dataset has to a tragic outcome, but these are typically already badly injured when picked up. Guinea pigs (33.7% adopted, 32.0% rescued, 27.9% transferred, 2.9% euthanised) and reptiles (61.6% rescued) have notably benign outcome distributions.

ana_09.label: Live-release rate by species — dogs over the line, cats just under
ana_09.content: Live-release rate by species (live = anything other than euthanasia / died / disposal / missing): dogs 92.5%, cats 77.7%, birds 68.9%, 'wild' 32.4%, 'other' 44.4%, rabbits 81.1%, reptiles 92.2%, guinea pigs 96.5%. Dogs comfortably clear the 90% no-kill bar; cats fall ~12 points short, dragged down primarily by neonates that arrive too young to survive without a queen and by feral adults that go through the TNR pathway rather than adoption. The wild-animal save rate of 32.4% should not be read alongside cat/dog rates — these animals usually arrive injured beyond rehabilitation and the alternative isn't adoption.

data_table.description: Live-release rate by species (excluding rows with missing outcome_type)

ana_10.label: Intake condition is the strongest single predictor of outcome
ana_10.content: Triage status at intake separates outcomes more cleanly than species or year does. Cats and dogs entering as 'normal' have a 95.3% live-release rate. 'Under age/weight' (mostly neonates) drops to 78.5%. 'Injured severe' falls to 30.7% and 'ill severe' to just 24.9%. 'Fractious' (often unsocialised cats) is 89.9% live-release because most go through TNR. 'Welfare seizures' (animals removed from cruelty cases) hit 100% live-release on n=65 — small sample but consistent with deliberate placement. The takeaway: the no-kill benchmark works well as a goal but it must be read alongside what walks in the door. A shelter that takes more severely-injured animals will have a lower headline rate even when its medical work is identical to a shelter that takes only 'normal' intake.

ana_11.label: Three-quarters arrive without an owner-given name
ana_11.content: Of 29,787 records, only 7,660 (25.7%) arrive with a name typed in by an owner. 9,965 (33.5%) start with an asterisk — given by shelter staff because the animal had no known name — and 12,162 (40.8%) are blank, meaning the animal was never given a name in the system at all. The asterisk and the blank are both consequences of the shelter taking in strays and wildlife rather than just owner surrenders.

data_table.description: Animal name status: how the animal entered the shelter

ana_12.label: The asterisk pattern is intake-type specific
ana_12.content: The naming convention precisely tracks how the animal arrived. Owner-surrender intakes are 76.8% owner-named — and 15.5% staff-named, presumably for animals whose owners surrendered them with no name on the paperwork. 'Wildlife' intakes are 97.0% blank — wildlife is rarely named at all. 'Stray' intakes are 35.3% blank, 21.8% owner-named (the 'lost pet' pattern, where the animal had a name on a tag), and 42.9% staff-named (truly anonymous strays who got 'Squiggles' from intake staff). 'Trap-neuter-return' intakes are 68.5% staff-named — the colony cat pattern. 'Adopted animal return' is 100% owner-named — the animal kept the name from its previous adoption file.

stray: blank 35.3, owner_named 21.8, staff_named 42.9

data_table.description: Distribution of name status (%) within each intake type

ana_13.label: Owner-named cats and dogs are 41% more likely to go home
ana_13.content: Owner-named cats and dogs return to their owner 41.3% of the time. Staff-named ones return to owner 0.8% of the time, and blank-named ones 0.8%. Conversely, staff-named animals are adopted out at 43.1% — much higher than the 24.7% rate for owner-named (who often go home instead of being adopted). The headline live-release rate is identical at 93.2% for both owner-named and staff-named, but blank-named animals drop to 61.7% — these are dominated by wildlife, where 'live release' simply isn't the right framing. The asterisk in the data dictionary turns out to be a clean proxy for 'arrived with a human attachment' that downstream behaviour confirms.

ana_15.label: Length of stay — adoption is the slow path
ana_15.content: Median length of stay for cats and dogs varies sharply by outcome. Adoptions take 27 days median, 48.5 days mean — the slowest live exit. Rescue/transfer pulls happen in 6 days median. Return-to-owner is the fastest: 1 day median, 3.9 days mean — most lost dogs are reunited within 24-48 hours. Euthanasia has a 0-day median (much of it is 'euthenasia required' day-of-intake for non-survivable wildlife or severe trauma cases). 'Foster to adopt' takes 12 days median. The 'missing' bucket has a 73.5-day median — these are animals whose paperwork drifted before resolution.

ana_18.label: Why people surrender pets
ana_18.content: Of 2,615 owner-surrender records, 857 (32.8%) have no reason recorded. Among the 1,758 with a reason: 'owner prob' leads at 405 (the catch-all for owner-side issues), then 'move' (231), 'landlord' (133, i.e. landlord prohibits pets), 'cost' (127), 'no time' (115), 'no home' (110, owner became unhoused), 'bites' (73), 'too many' (66, often after unplanned litters), 'agg animal' (58), 'allergic' (56), 'owner died' (55), 'ill' (54), 'abandon' (34), 'agg people' (32), 'poor helth' (31), 'other pet' (22), 'new baby' (13). The top four reasons together — owner-prob, move, landlord, cost — are housing- and economics-driven, accounting for ~896 surrenders (~51% of those with a reason). 'New baby' is one of the smallest categories, contradicting the common worry that pets are surrendered when children arrive.

ana_19.content: By jurisdiction: Long Beach 25,590 (85.9%), Cerritos 2,023 (6.8%), Signal Hill 721 (2.4%), Los Alamitos 531 (1.8%), Seal Beach 373 (1.3%), Out of Area 218, plus a long tail of LA County (52), Orange County (50), and other small jurisdictions. The four contracted neighbour cities together — Cerritos, Signal Hill, Los Alamitos, Seal Beach — contribute 12.3% of intake.

ana_20.label: Quarterly intake — granular pandemic shape
ana_20.content: Quarterly intake reveals more shape than the annual view. The pre-pandemic baseline runs around 1,200-1,500 animals per quarter through 2017-2019. Q1 2020 drops to 452 — the first lockdown quarter — and intake stays under 800/quarter until Q2 2022, when it returns to 1,323. The 2024 peak quarter is Q2 (1,587), April-June, perfectly aligned with kitten season. Q4 quarters (October-December) consistently sit ~30% below their corresponding Q2.

data_table.description: Quarterly intake counts, 2017Q1 to 2024Q4

ana_21.label: Intake hotspot ZIPs
ana_21.content: Embedding ZIP codes in the crossing/address strings allows mapping intake by ZIP. The top 5 ZIPs are 90805 (5,672 intakes — North Long Beach including Bixby Knolls borders), 90813 (3,024 — Central Long Beach / Cambodia Town), 90806 (2,583 — Wrigley / Bixby Knolls south), 90815 (2,334 — Los Altos / Stearns Park), 90703 (1,898 — Cerritos). 90805 alone accounts for 19.0% of all intake with a known ZIP. These are dense, lower-income, family neighbourhoods where stray density is empirically highest.

data_table.description: Intake counts by ZIP code (top 12)

ana_23.label: The single hottest intake block is the shelter itself
ana_23.content: Hex-binning intake coordinates at 0.005 degrees (~500 m) reveals a striking artefact: the single highest-density bin sits at 33.810N, -118.085W with 560 intakes — the location of the P.D. Pitchford Companion Animal Village shelter in El Dorado Park East. Many crossing addresses default to the shelter's own coordinates when a precise pickup location wasn't recorded (e.g., owner-surrender walk-ins). The next densest bins — 33.770/-118.195, 33.790/-118.190, 33.775/-118.180 — fall in central and west Long Beach, where genuine intake density is highest.

data_table.description: Top 12 intake-density 500m hex bins (lat, lon, count)

caveats.content: The dataset spans 2017-2024 but the year-over-year comparison is sensitive to which date column is used. ana_01 / ana_05 / ana_20 use intake_date; ana_02 / ana_03 / ana_04 use outcome_date. Animals taken in late one year and adopted early the next will appear in different years across the two views — this is correct, not a bug, but it should be flagged.
187 rows (0.6%) have a missing outcome_type. These are excluded from save-rate computations. Their inclusion would change cat/dog 2024 save_pct by less than 0.5 points.

Live-release rate here counts everything that is NOT in {euthanasia, died, disposal, missing} as live. This is conservative; some shelters exclude wildlife and owner-requested euthanasia from the denominator, which would raise the headline rate.
ZIP codes were extracted by regex from the free-text crossing column, so a small number of mis-formatted addresses are missing a ZIP. ana_21 reflects the ~93% of rows where extraction succeeded.
Geographic coordinates frequently snap to the shelter address when the intake location wasn't recorded (ana_23). Treat the single hottest bin as an artefact rather than a real hotspot.

The data cannot causally attribute changes to the 2019 Compassion Saves policy or to COVID; both interventions coincide with the trends. Use 'coincides with' / 'after' rather than 'because of' when referencing them.
